Please enjoy Day 15 of the series.
Gordon Jones of Maysville is an author, pastor and teacher.
Jones has written autobiographies, historical books, technical books, murder mysteries and children's books.
He stated that he has been writing for a long time but only started writing books recently.
'I have been writing letters to prisoners and the downtrodden for years. I have written poems and a Christmas play. However, my first of four books was written in 2022 and I have no rear-view mirror,' said Jones.
He explained that he has always loved to read although few in his family felt the same way.
'I had great English teachers and read many of the classics when I was a teenager and also read all of the Sherlock Holmes books written by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle,' said Jones. 'I was the villain in the Maysville High School senior play. My family is also full of storytellers. I believe all these experiences led me to write.'
Jones noted that writing gives him to opportunity to express his feelings. He refers to writing as 'very cathartic' and explained that it has helped him to 'recover from early family issues and loss in my early life.'
'My ultimate goal would be to show people what matters most in life,' explained Jones.
To find out more about Jones's craft, he stated to simply reach out to him personally.
He included that his books are available for purchase from Christian Treasures, Kenton Stories, Sprinkles of Hope, Amazon, Barnes and Noble or they can be checked out at the library.
Jones was born and raised in Maysville. In his early life, he attended Maysville High School and later attended the University of Kentucky. Jones taught at the Maysville Community and Technical College for 13 years and is also the pastor at Shepherd's House Church.
Jones' books include Divinely Encountered, The Son Also Rises, WWII: The Fighting Faris Family, and Power In The Clouds.
Additionally, he is in the process of writing Ghosts In The Sky, Murder On Market Street and The Lonely Christmas Tree.

title: Fite commits to Shelton State
description: Mason County senior Cray Fite has committed to Shelton State Community College, to continue his baseball and academic careers.
content:
Mason County senior Cray Fite has committed to Shelton State Community College, to continue his baseball and academic careers.
Fite began his baseball career with the Royals his freshman year, in 2022. That year, he saw 31 games as a hitter, and picked up 31 hits across 90 at-bats for a .344 batting average. He also scored 24 runs for Mason County, and batted in 26, walking 15 times and striking out just 27. On the mound that year, Fite threw in seven games, for 23.2 innings, striking out 20 and allowing 16 runs, ending his freshman year with a 3.25 ERA.
His sophomore year in 2023, Fite saw 100 at-bats, picking up 30 hits for an even .300 batting average. That year he made it home 23 times, batting in 26 for the Royals, with just 19 strikeouts on the season. As a pitcher he saw 10 games, pitching 38 innings. That year he gave up 39 hits and 18 runs, and ended his second season with a 2.73 ERA.
Last year, Fite was a crucial element in Mason County's historic run through the 10th region baseball tournament, helping his team come away with their first 10th region championship since 1994.
At the end of the 2024 season, Fite was the Royals' strongest hitter, picking up 46 hits across 116 at-bats for a .397 batting average. He ended the season with a career high 33 runs, batting in 42 for the Royals, with just 16 strikeouts, 11 base-on-balls, and five hit-by-pitches. Fite was also Mason County's second strongest pitcher last season, throwing in 57.1 innings for Mason County across nine games. He allowed 42 hits and 29 runs, 21 earned. He also picked up 41 strikeouts, with an ERA of 2.56 on the season.
He was the team's sole pitcher in the 2024 10th region championship game, throwing all seven innings, allowing just four hits and no runs that game. In the batters box, he picked up one hit, and two RBI's, helping secure Mason County's 8-0 win over Bourbon County.
Throughout his high-school career so far, Fite has picked up a career batting average of .350, and a career ERA of 3.55, making him one of Mason County's strongest both on the mound and in the batters-box. Looking ahead to his final season with the Mason County Royals, Fite is excited to continue playing baseball at the high-school level, as he looks to end his career with even stronger stats offensively and defensively.
Come the 2026 baseball season, Fite will see his first collegiate baseball game, where he looks to become as valuable an asset to the Buccaneers.

title: Babz Bites: Best Bites of 2024 (Part 2)
author: Chef Babz Nartowicz
description: The readers of this Babz Bites love to eat real food. Food that represents the Ohio River Valley and isn't just the same commercialized something that can be found any place. Our community is special…
content:
The readers of this Babz Bites love to eat real food. Food that represents the Ohio River Valley and isn't just the same commercialized something that can be found any place. Our community is special and it shows in how we eat, where we eat and what we eat.
As a river valley community the Appalachian foothills add a unique culinary touch to our kitchen tables. Our gardens grow in different directions but along the same river. This can be attributed to the variety of heritage and backgrounds the people of the river valley stem from. Our area has always been an artistic enclave harvesting its own renaissance and flavors. We don't just create, we pull-up an extra chair to our table.
Give the second half of the Best Bites of 2024 a look, and maybe a taste. Let me know if there is
something you'd like to explore together next year!
Good luck and happy New Year!
July
Roasted chicken with sumac, olives and lemon
4 chicken leg quarters
4 cloves garlic, crushed
1 red onion, sliced
1/4 cup pomegranate molasses
2 tablespoons sumac powder
1/2 teaspoons ground cinnamon
1 Meyer lemon, thinly sliced
1/4 cup pitted green olives and brine
1/4 cup olive oil
2 tablespoons pine nuts
8 ounces water (or chicken stock)
Salt to taste
Flat-leaf parsley
Pat chicken legs dry and marinate with 2 tablespoons of olive oil, salt, olives and with brine,
spices, lemon juice and pomegranate molasses. Let sit for a couple of hours. Preheat the oven to
375 degrees. Heat a Dutch oven or large cast iron pan and add remaining oil. Add onions and
cook until they just start to brown. Add the crushed garlic and continue to cook until just brown.
Add chicken, skin side up, along with pine nuts and enough liquid to cover the bottom of the
pan. Place in the oven for 45 minutes to one hour or until chicken is cooked to 165 degrees.
Finish with a liberal amount of freshly chopped parsley. Serve with a bright-green salad, roasted
potatoes and thick yogurt with za'atar.
August
Norma's Old-Fashioned Peach Cobbler
From the kitchen of Norma Linville.
'I like that it uses very little refined sugar, but uses apple juice instead,' said Norma, who credits The Healthy Heart Cookbook she was given in 1983, with the recipe.
¼ cup cornstarch
¼ cup unsweetened apple juice
10 cups sliced fresh peaches
1 cup unsweetened apple juice
½ cup sugar
½ tsp ground nutmeg
½ tsp almond extract
½ cup all-purpose flour
⅛ tsp salt
⅛ tsp ground nutmeg
2 Tbsp margarine
1 to 1 ½ Tbsp cold water
1 Tbsp all-purpose flour
Vegetable cooking spray
Fresh mint sprig (optional)
Combine cornstarch and ¼ apple juice; stir well, and set aside.
Combine peaches, 1 cup apple juice, sugar, and 1/2 tsp nutmeg in a Dutch oven. Bring to a boil;
cover, reduce heat, and simmer 8 to 10 minutes or until peaches are tender. Stir in reserved
cornstarch mixture. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened and bubbly. Remove from heat,
and stir in almond extract.
Let cool.
Combine ½ cup flour, salt, and 1/8 tsp nutmeg in a medium bowl; cut in margarine with a pastry
blender until mixture resembles coarse meal. Sprinkle cold water, 1 Tbsp at a time, over surface;
stir with a fork just until dry ingredients are moistened. Shape dough into a ball.
Sprinkle 1 Tbsp flour evenly over work surface. Roll dough to an 8-inch square floured surface;
cut into ½-inch strips.
Spoon peach mixture into an 8-inch square baking dish coated with cooking spray. Arrange
pastry strips lattice-style over peach mixture. Seal pastry to edge of dish. Bake at 425 degrees for
20 minutes or until pastry is golden and filling is bubbly. Garnish with a fresh mint sprig, if
desired. Serve warm.
September
Pawpaw Lassi
Created by the chefs at Casa Nueva Restaurant in Athens, Ohio. Winner of 'Best Drink' at the
1999 Ohio Pawpaw Festival.
Makes about six cups.
½ cup water
4 cups plain yogurt
⅔ cup honey
½ tsp salt
1 cup pawpaw pulp
½ tsp ground cinnamon
Blend together all ingredients until smooth. Serve cold.
October
Roast Carrot & Coconut Soup
Serves 4-6
One of my favorite tools in the kitchen as of late is the immersion blender. If you don't have one,
treat yourself because it is well worth it and the clean up is even easier.
8 large carrots, just chopped not skinned
1 large sweet potato, or 2 small
2 small white potatoes
5 large cloves garlic
2 medium onion
2-3 tablespoons olive oil
Salt and pepper to taste
2 teaspoons turmeric, ground
1 can coconut milk
1 cup water
In a large pan, add olive oil, garlic and onions to medium heat. After about 3 minutes, add
carrots and potatoes. Cover pot to allow moisture to remain. Every few minutes stir so that
veggies do not stick to the bottom of the pan.
After all the veggies are thoroughly cooked, turn off the burner. The veggies will be soft and
will probably begin to mush up when you stir them. This will probably take about 30
minutes.
If you have an immersion blender, stick it in the pot and blend veggies. If not, add half of the
veggies to a blender with half the portions included in this recipe for water, coconut milk,
and turmeric. Blend. Do this one more time with the remaining veggies and portions.
Pour blended mix into a crock pot if you want to keep things at a slow cooking heat to serve
or a large pot. I prefer the crockpot because it allows me to make this hours before serving.
Soup may also be put into a storage container and placed in the fridge or freezer to eat at a
later time.
Dill and rosemary make a lovely garnish, but if you have time make some bacon and dice it up
then roll in brown sugar. Even try sprinkling a little Asiago on the brown sugar bacon. It really
makes a delicious treat for guests.
November
Tibetan Autumn Soup (Thenthuk)
Traditionally, Thenthuk would be made with meat, but the nuns in India eat a vegetarian diet.
This is a meat-optional recipe. Thenthuk is one particular kind of Tibetan noodle soup. Its name
means pull-noodle soup.
Serves 2-4
Noodle Dough
1 heaping cup all-purpose flour
1/2 cup water, room temperature
1/4 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp pepper
1 tsp oil
Broth
2 or 3 tbsp vegetable oil
1 clove garlic, finely chopped
1 tbsp ginger, finely minced
1 small onion, chopped
1 carrot, chopped into thin strips
1 large tomato, roughly chopped
4 to 5 cups vegetable or other stock
2 green/spring onions, chopped
cilantro, a few sprigs, roughly chopped
handful of spinach
soy sauce or salt to taste
Noodle Instructions
In a bowl, combine the dough ingredients, mix well and then knead for 4 minutes. Cover and
leave to stand for 5 minutes. Roll or flatten out the dough and cut into long strips and then make
the broth.
Soup Instructions
In a large pot on medium heat, sauté garlic, ginger, and onion in oil for 1 minute. Add carrots
and tomato and gently sauté for one minute. Add most of the stock and bring to a boil. Adjust the
amount of stock later depending on the soup to noodle ratio you prefer.
Put the noodle in the soup by draping the strips over your hand and tearing off pieces of about an
inch in size, throwing them into the boiling soup. Cook for 2 minutes until the noodles are
cooked and the stock is boiling. Add the chopped green onions, cilantro, and spinach and cook
for about 30 seconds. Season with soy sauce or salt. Serve immediately.
December
Hot Cranberry Drink
Delicious Suggestion: Add Bourbon & garnish with lemon slices & or Rosemary sprigs
6-8 cups
1 tbsp whole cloves
3 2-inch cinnamon sticks, broken
2 cups cranberry juice cocktail
2 cups unsweetened pineapple juice
1/2 teaspoon whole allspice
1/3 light brown sugar
Put liquids and brown sugar in the bottom of the percolator. Put spices on top of the
percolator. Perk 10 minutes. Serve in hot punch cups garnished. Do not pour hot punch into a
glass punch bowl. If it's too hot, it will break.

title: Supreme Court of Kentucky issues public reprimand for Tolle
description: The Supreme Court of Kentucky issued a public reprimand regarding Mason County Circuit Court Clerk Kirk Tolle after his arrest and conviction.
content:
The Supreme Court of Kentucky issued a public reprimand regarding Mason County Circuit Court Clerk Kirk Tolle after his arrest and conviction.
The Circuit Court Clerk Conduct Commission is in place to ensure that clerks hold themselves to a high level of 'integrity, impartiality, and independence to promote public confidence in the judicial system,' stated the reprimand.
On May 28, 2024, Mason County Sheriff Ryan Swolsky responded to a call regarding an individual who appeared to be under the influence of alcohol.
According to Tolle's arrest citation, upon arriving at the scene Swolsky determined that Tolle's pupils were dilated and that Tolle was unable to maintain his balance and 'stepped off the line and took an incorrect number of steps.'
He further noted that Tolle insisted he had had one drink that morning and had taken no medications or substances nor did he have any prior injuries or balance issues.
Tolle was arrested and charged with operating a motor vehicle under the influence of alcohol in the second offense (non-aggravated).
After his arrest, Tolle took a voluntary leave of absence. During this time, the Chief Justice appointed a sitting clerk from a neighboring circuit to serve as Special Circuit Clerk stated the reprimand.
The document stated that the Commission requested that Tolle file a written response.
'In his response, Mr. Tolle acknowledged the existence of the uniform citation report and stated that the criminal case against him was still pending,' read the document. 'Mr. Tolle also indicated that, after taking a leave of absence, he sought counseling with a licensed counselor and an organization with experience with substance use disorders and attended several lawyer-based Alcoholics Anonymous meetings.'
Tolle also pointed out in his statement that he had served as the Mason County Circuit Clerk for almost 24 years with no prior incident.
According to Supreme Court of Kentucky documents, the Commission submitted its findings and recommendations to the Chief Justice under Section 8(6) of AP Part XVI and found that the following violations against the Code of Conduct for Circuit Court Clerks were made;
'Section 4(1)3: Clerk Tolle violated the section of the Code of Conduct by being under the influence of alcohol while he was working on May 28, 2024, and could not have fulfilled and adequately performed his duties as circuit clerk while under the influence of alcohol,' and 'Section 5(1)4: Clerk Kirk Tolle violated this section of the Code of Conduct by being under the influence of alcohol while he was working on Court of Justice property (Mason Circuit Cler's office) on May 28, 2024. While Clerk Tolle was charged with DUI second and has not been convicted of said charge, his response to the Complaint against him does not dispute that he was intoxicated while at work on May 28, 2024.'
The reprimand documents continued and expressed that the Commission recommended to the Chief Justice that the following disciplinary action should be taken;
'(1) Clerk Tolle should remain on voluntary leave of absence with pay, or if he does not choose to remain on voluntary leave, he should be formally suspended by the Chief Justice until adjudication of his DUI second case (24-T-489)[;]' (2) 'Clerk Tolle should be issued a Public Reprimand[;]' '(3) 'Clerk Tolle should receive a substance abuse assessment by a licensed substance and alcohol abuse provider and follow any treatment recommendations[;]' and (4) 'Clerk Tolle should file a report of his treatment provider evidencing compliance with treatment recommendations every sixty (60) days to the Chief Justice's office for a period of one year.'
Per the public reprimand, since the Commission's recommendation, Tolle has pleaded guilty to an amended charge of operating a motor vehicle under the influence of alcohol in the first offense.
According to the reprimand, Tolle was sentenced by the court to '30 days of imprisonment, with 23 days conditionally discharged for two years, and seven days to serve on home incarceration from Jan. 2 through Jan. 8, 2025.'
Additionally, The Commission has the authority to recommend a variety of disciplinary measures that could be imposed by the Chief Justice.
'While circuit clerks are elected officials, they are also 'personnel within the Court of Justice' and are 'subject to the administrative control of the Chief Justice,'' per KRS 30A.010(2).
The Chief Justice ordered the following in the reprimand;
'Mason County Circuit Court Clerk Kirk Tolle is publicly reprimanded for the violations of the Code of Conduct for the Circuit Court Clerks noted above.'
Mr. Tolle shall be formally suspended, with pay, for 60 days, with credit for time served on administrative leave.
Mr. Tolle may return to the Mason Circuit Court Clerk's Office upon the conclusion of his term of home incarceration as ordered in Commonwealth v. Edward K. Tolle, 24-T-00489 (Mason Dist. Ct. filed May 29, 2024).
Mr. Tolle shall receive a substance use evaluation from a licensed addiction counselor and follow any treatment plan developed by the counselor.
He shall also submit to the Chief Justice a treatment plan progress report from his addiction counselor every 60 days for a period of six months from the date of this order.
Lastly, Mr. Tolle according to the reprimand, 'shall not retaliate against any person who, in good faith, made a report or otherwise assisted in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing conducted in connection to the violations of the Code of Conduct for Circuit Court Clerks noted above. Under KRS 30A.010(2) and Ky. Const. § 110(5)(b), the Chief Justice may impose additional disciplinary measures if Mr. Tolle fails to comply with this order.'
This reprimand was issued and signed by Kentucky Chief Justice Laurance B. VanMeter on Jan. 2, 2025.

title: Maysville Area Chamber of Commerce highlights 2024
description: The Maysville Area Chamber of Commerce discussed and highlighted a year of success in 2024.
content:
The Maysville Area Chamber of Commerce discussed and highlighted a year of success in 2024.
Chamber Executive Kaci Foster expressed that the year had been, 'marked by collaboration, innovation and a shared commitment to the growth and vitality of our community.'
According to the Chamber, in 2024, it grew its First Friday Coffee networking series, held its most attended State Legislature Update, and hosted the largest Women's Leadership Summit.
'We proudly hosted over 50 events designed to connect, educate and celebrate our business community,' the Chamber stated.
It further acknowledged that over $30,000 was invested into the community through events and programming allowing the Chamber to expand opportunities for items such as education, advocacy and engagement.
In 2024 the Chamber introduced a few new partner benefits including a Partner Portal, Partner Savings Program and a Love Local Campaign.
The Partner Portal allows partners of the Chamber to control their benefits including features like updating directory profiles, posting jobs, sharing news, posting special deals and adding events to a community calendar as well as registering for events.
Through the Partner Savings Program, partners with the Chamber have the ability to access exclusive discounts and offers that are from Chamber members.
According to the Chamber, the Love Local Campaign was, 'created to celebrate and support the businesses that make our community unique.' Additionally the initiative, 'encouraged residents to shop, dine and engage with local businesses, emphasizing the critical role they play in our economy,' the Chamber stated.
The Chamber further expressed;
'The Love Local Campaign exemplifies our commitment to strengthening the connection between businesses and residents, ensuring a thriving local economy for years to come,' said the Chamber.
For the new year of 2025, the Chamber stated that there are five opportunities to come including expanded programming, Chamber Foundation launch, enhanced partner benefits, regional collaboration and Leadership Horizons 2025.
'The 2024 Annual Report reflects the dedication and collaboration of our Chamber, our Partners, and our community. We are proud of the statewide recognition we've received and the progress we've made together over the past year. This report is a celebration of our shared success and a reminder of the exciting opportunities ahead as we continue to build on this momentum,' Foster stated.
(This article was updated on Jan. 17.)

title: Shootout at high noon in Rupp
author: Chuck Hamilton
description: In what is expected to be an entertaining, high-scoring affair between two highly ranked teams, Alabama and Kentucky will be looking to drain as many three-point bombs as they can beginning at noon today. If successful, the Rupp Arena nets may have to be replaced after being scorched by the longtime Southeastern Conference combatants.
content:
In what is expected to be an entertaining, high-scoring affair between two highly ranked teams, Alabama and Kentucky will be looking to drain as many three-point bombs as they can beginning at noon today. If successful, the Rupp Arena nets may have to be replaced after being scorched by the longtime Southeastern Conference combatants.
The two teams aren't bashful when it comes to letting it fly from deep; Alabama is knocking down 10 threes per game, while UK is at 10.1. The Crimson Tide is jacking up 31.2 threes per outing, and the Cats 27.7, giving the visitors a percentage of 31.2, and Kentucky 36.5. Both teams have been filling it up in their first 17 games of the year as well, with the visitors tied with Iowa for the highest scoring offense in the nation at 89.5 points per game, and UK next at 88.7.
Coach Nate Oats and his squad are ranked fourth in the latest AP poll, and they will bring added incentive into the game after falling 74-64 at home on Tuesday to Ole Miss. Add that bit of motivation to the revenge factor for Alabama, which was shellacked last year in Rupp, 117-95. The teams enter with identical 14-3 overall marks and 3-1 in SEC play. Auburn and Ole Miss are the current league co-leaders with 4-0 records, with Tennessee and Missouri at 3-1.
One key to a Kentucky victory will be containing two-time All-SEC guard Mark Sears, who is tossing in 18.6 points per game to go with 4.5 assists. The 6-1 lefty can get on a roll in a hurry, and UK point guard Lamont Butler will have his hands full. Butler is also banged up after injuring his shoulder in the Cats' win over
Texas A&M on Tuesday, which could affect his minutes against the Tide.
While Sears, an Ohio University transfer, is the catalyst for the Alabama offense, he has plenty of scoring assistance. Grant Nelson, a 6-11 grad student, averages 12 ppg and is the team's leading rebounder with 8.6 per game. Other double-digit point producers include 6-4 freshman Labaron Philon (11.4) and 6-1 Auburn transfer Aden Holloway (11.1).
Kentucky hopes to capitalize on Alabama's perceived weaknesses, which include a penchant for turnovers and defending without fouling. The Crimson Tide committed 21 miscues in the loss to Ole Miss, giving the Rebels 23 more field goal attempts. In SEC play, Alabama has fouled their opponents nearly 21 times per game, giving their foes nearly 27 free throws per game. UK needs convert at the stripe if given the opportunity in what should be a close game. They have been up and down at the line, but they are converting 73.9% overall.
A positive aspect of Alabama's game is hitting the offensive glass. They have been outrebounded just once in their 17 games this season. It will be imperative for the Cats to limit extra opportunities by hitting the boards and perhaps turning the tables on the Tide with efficient offensive rebounding themselves.
Kentucky is hoping Jaxson Robinson continues his hot shooting streak after back-to-back productive performances. The 6-6 guard has led the team with 23 and 22-point efforts in wins over Mississippi State and A&M. The Cats are also looking for Koby Brea to break out of his recent shooting slump and return to the form he showed in the team's 106-100 win over Florida.
Otega Oweh has been a consistent offensive force, scoring in double figures in every game, and Amari Williams is showing improvement, especially on the glass in recent games.
As this blurb is being written, odds have yet to be set for this one, but it says here that the Cats should be a slight favorite on their home court. If head coach Mark Pope can keep his squad focused and playing well, there's no telling what this veteran group can accomplish. They seldom get rattled, and the only real low point thus far has been the loss to Ohio State, but even the best teams lay an egg once in a while.
Kentucky knows teams want to bully them and play a physical style, but if the win over a rough bunch of Aggies is any indication, the Cats can dish it out as well. Going through the SEC gauntlet should act as solid preparation for the postseason, as long as they don't suffer key injuries while playing in the premier league in college basketball.
*****
RAVENS-BILLS HIGHLIGHTS NFL SLATE – The National Football League is down to its own version of the 'Elite Eight,' with a pair of games slated for today, and two more on Sunday. The NFL is hoping these games will be much more competitive than what proved to be a boring Wild Card Weekend.
The first matchup features the two-time defending champion Kansas City Chiefs hosting the Houston Texans this afternoon. Not many folks are giving the Texans much of a chance, but this may just turn out to be the upset of the weekend.
At 8 p.m. tonight, the consensus NFC favorite Detroit Lions host one of the most surprising teams in the NFL this season, the Washington Commanders. On a personal note, I'm pulling for
coach Dan Quinn and rookie quarterback Jayden Daniels to upend the Lions, but my head says that ain't gonna happen.
The Sunday games will have the LA Rams visiting Philadelphia at 3 p.m., and the Eagles will prevail in what is predicted to be a game played in miserable, chilly, rainy conditions.
The final game of the NFL Divisional Round will be held in lovely Buffalo, where the Bills will host the Baltimore Ravens in what close observers and talking heads say will be the best game of the weekend. It's hard to argue that point, but sometimes expectations don't live up to what occurs on the field. This is another one where I admittedly have a rooting preference; I'm pulling for the Bills to knock off the Ravens, and I think they'll get it done in a thriller.
*****
IRISH HOPE TO SLOW BUCKEYES' PASSING ATTACK – The inaugural expanded 12-team College Football Playoff is down to two teams, with both having tons of rooting interest in this area.
On Monday evening in Atlanta, the favored Ohio State Buckeyes will look to finish off an impressive stretch of overwhelming wins and defeat the Fighting Irish of Notre Dame. The Bucks enter as an 8.5-point pick to win their ninth national title, and their second in the CFP era. The Irish have claimed 11 national championships, with the last one coming in 1988.
Both 2025 versions of these tradition-rich programs are highlighted by stout defenses and effective ground games, but the Buckeyes have the clear edge in the passing game. This one will likely come down to which team wins the line of scrimmage
and the team with the least mistakes will come out on top. I realize the previous sentence sounds oh so cliché, but that's the way I see it.
If Notre Dame can keep the Ohio State passing attack in check, they have a great shot at winning No. 12, but if not, it will be party time in Columbus.
*****
'There was no three-minute run where we felt great where we felt like we really got into a flow. For our guys to win that game is really important. I like the way we can win different ways. I'm proud of the effort on the glass and on the defensive end. And we still can get so much better.' – Mark Pope, following the Cats' 81-69 grind-it-out win over Texas A&M
*****
'Any time Detroit scores more than hundred points and holds the other team below a hundred points, they almost always win.' – Doug Collins
***** 'There is in life only one moment and in eternity only one. It is so brief that it is represented by the fleeting of a luminous mote through the thin ray of sunlight – and it is visible but a fraction of a second. The moments that preceded it have been lived, are forgotten and are without value; the moments that have not been lived have no existence and will have no value except in the moment that each shall be lived. While you are asleep you are dead, and whether you stay dead an hour or a billion years the time to you is the same.' — Mark Twain

title: Reed to join the Indians against Mason County Saturday
description: The Mason County Royals will face off against the Montgomery County Indians this Saturday at the Lake Kelly Classic in Fleming County.
content:
The Mason County Royals will face off against the Montgomery County Indians this Saturday at the Lake Kelly Classic in Fleming County.
Montgomery County, the new home of former Royal Cayden Reed sits at 7-8 on the season, with a points per game average of 62.7. Although Reed has been ineligible for play since the start of the season, this will mark his first contest with the Indians, and he is eager to tip off against Mason County when they take the floor of the Panther Den this weekend.
Reed started his varsity career at Bracken County, totalling 126 points for the Polar Bears as a seventh grader. The following year he put up 287 as an eighth grader, 586 as a freshman and 482 as a sophomore. Last season with the Royals, Reed totalled 251, and remained one of Mason County's top five scorers despite his departure from the team midway through the season.
Currently, the Indians are led in scoring by Tyce Jarvis. The sophomore has totalled 261 points on the season to average 17.5, sitting with a 41.5% field goal average having gone 97 for 234.
Mason County sits at 7-7 on the season right now, averaging 63.1 points per game. Braeden Myrick leads the offense for the Royals, with 238 total points on the season to average 17.0 per game. Myrick has gone 82 for 172 this year, sitting with a 47.7% field goal average.
Both teams will hit the court Saturday afternoon hungry to pull out a win in the Lake Kelly Classic. Before then however, both the Royals and Indians have several games on the schedule throughout the week. Mason County has two contests prior to their game with the Indians, their first a game on the road tomorrow against the 9-5 Bourbon County Colonels, followed by a district seed game at the Fieldhouse on Thursday against the 5-12 Bracken County Polar Bears.
Montgomery County will host the 8-10 Paris Greyhounds tomorrow, before heading to Campbell County on Thursday to take on the 12-3 Camels.
The two teams will then head to Flemingsburg Saturday afternoon to take on one another, scheduled for a 2:00 p.m. tipoff. This contest will prove to be a tough challenge for both teams, and will likely be a highly competitive environment.
Other teams in attendance will include the Lewis County Lions, Scott Eagles, Cooper Jaguars and tournament hosts, the Fleming County Panthers.

title: Lady Royals clinch the one seed
description: The Mason County Lady Royals hosted the Bracken County Lady Bears in their second meeting of the 2024-25 season.
content:
The Mason County Lady Royals hosted the Bracken County Lady Bears in their second meeting of the 2024-25 season.
In the first game of a boy/ girl doubleheader, the Lady Royals and Lady Bears took the floor of the Fieldhouse to play their second of two 39th district seed contests. In their first meeting of the year, Mason County came out ahead of the reigning 39th district champions 57-47 at Bracken County's home gym. This go around, the Lady Royals were hoping to once again pull out a victory over the Lady Bears, and secure the number one seed.
Bracken County got off to a strong start early in the contest, with Nicole Archibald putting up six, and both Jenna Colvin and Brianna Bauer two apiece to total ten points by the end of the first quarter.
Despite picking up an early lead, the Lady Bears would fall behind by the end of the first eight minutes of play, with the Lady Royals outscoring Bracken County 15-10. In the first, Amirah Reed had six, Olivia Hughes five, and both Adrienne Downs-Perry and Lexi Young two, to round out Mason County's scoring in this quarter.
'We definitely got off to a good early start. We tried to switch some things up defensively, slow them down a little bit.' said Lady Royals head coach, Jay Fite.
Heading into the second quarter, Mason County was looking to hold onto their five point lead over the Lady Bears, while Bracken County hoped to pull out ahead as the first half came to a close.
The Lady Royals defense successfully held off Bracken County's strong offense in the second quarter, holding the Lady Bears to six. This quarter, Mason County outscored the Lady Bears 11-6, with a trio of threes from Hughes, Kyliegh Kirk and Carlee Buttery totalling nine, and two more from Reed to close out the scoring this quarter.
'When she gets it going, she really has it. We definitely want her to be confident, we definitely want her looking for open opportunities. We try to find some little seams in our offense for her to get to the rim, and we like her taking the three ball as well.' said coach Fite, 'Tonight, she did it from the perimeter and she got to the seams as well. We finally got a few things going in transition, when she's going it kinda opens things up for others as well.'
Mason County led 26-16 heading into halftime, a ten point lead the Lady Royals hoped to hold onto throughout the remainder of the contest.
Bracken County, however, refused to quit and began going to work offensively to try and close the point deficit. This quarter, the Lady Bears outscored Mason County 16-12, bringing the game close multiple times throughout the third quarter. The Lady Bears unfortunately though were unable to get out ahead of the Lady Royals, and headed into the final eight minutes of the contest down six, Mason County leading 38-32.
'That third quarter they started to knock some shots down, against our zone. We tried to adjust back, they got it back to three, I think we got it back to a little comfortable lead. We didn't handle it super well in our late game situation, but we made some big shots, Amirah made some threes, helped extend the lead.' said coach Fite.
Throughout the fourth, Bracken County continued to fight to try to bring the game out in their favor, but the Lady Royals were just as hungry for the win. Both teams' offenses went to work this quarter, looking to put up big numbers for their team. By the time the quarter came to a close, both Mason County and Bracken County had scored 23, allowing the Lady Royals to come away with a six point lead, winning 61-55.
'We had kinda zoned up for a little bit, and obviously we had to start finding their shooters again, so we kinda matched back up man to man. We know they're good at penetrating and they've got enough shooters to make you stay wide. Bauer's a presence on the inside, they shoot free throws well, they're just kinda dangerous on different levels. Bracken's a good basketball team, they've been in it with the region's best all year, we're fortunate to get away with a win.' said coach Fite.
Now 5-0 in the district, Mason County has clinched the number one seed, with just one more district game left on the schedule, a contest against the Augusta Lady Panthers this coming Wednesday.
'I believe that puts us at the number one, that broke any tie breaker with them we would've had. That was a good one for us to have. When you seed the district, those are big. Moving forward, we've gotta continue to work on some late game situations, and taking care of the basketball down the stretch, but all in all it was good that we had a comfortable lead before we got to that point.' said coach Fite.

title: Reds Caravan stops in Maysville
author: Chuck Hamilton
description: As part of the annual pilgrimage taken by professional baseball's oldest franchise, one of the three Reds Caravan groups dispersed into Reds Country paid a media visit to Maysville last Friday morning.
content:
As part of the annual pilgrimage taken by professional baseball's oldest franchise, one of the three Reds Caravan groups dispersed into Reds Country paid a media visit to Maysville last Friday morning.
The entourage, which included president of baseball operations Nick Krall, manager Terry Francona, broadcaster Jim Day, roving minor league instructor and former Reds catcher Corky Miller, catcher Jose Trevino, outfielder Jacob Hurtubise, 19-year-old minor league catcher Alfredo Duno and mascot Mr. Red, was in town to visit Reds on Radio affiliate WFTM. They were greeted by invited guests at the Limestone Center to shake hands, pose for pictures, sign autographs and chat with the attendees.
Day introduced each member of the group, with the new Cincy skipper understandably receiving the warmest reception. The personable Francona is one of the most well-respected and successful managers in Major League Baseball history. He led the Boston Red Sox to its first world championship in 86 years in 2004, and added another title in 2007 during his eight-year stint in Boston. In his 11 seasons as Cleveland's manager, Francona led his teams to six playoff appearances, including the 2016 American League pennant.
Cincinnati fans are hoping the 65-year-old can bring their beloved Redlegs the same type of success and add to his Hall of Fame managing resume after he was coaxed out of retirement. Francona has compiled a career record of 1950-1672 during his 23 years as a big-league manager, and he needs 59 regular
season wins to pass Leo Durocher and move into 12th place on the all-time list.
The Reds Caravan made 14 fan stops in Ohio, Kentucky, Indiana and West Virginia to meet with fans over an eight-day period, spreading the news about the upcoming season while answering questions and signing autographs. The group that visited Maysville also traveled to Louisville's Slugger Field later on Friday, before going to the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green and the Red Mile in Lexington on Saturday.
It's always a treat for frozen baseball fans to look ahead to warmer temperatures and the upcoming season, and the Reds Caravan has become a welcome regional tradition. The Reds organization enjoys a special longtime connection with their radio partners, which is why they value stopping in Maysville while they make their rounds around the commonwealth and beyond.
On a personal note, I always look forward to the annual visit, and thanks go out to Travis Scaggs, the sports director at WFTM for the invite. For more information, check out his interviews with members of the entourage that will be airing on Soft96 in the coming days.
The visit is also an excellent opportunity to visit with Reds fans in the community, and talking with Mark Carpenter, the sports editor at the People's Defender in West Union, Ohio is always a personal highlight of the annual event.
*****
SHORTHANDED CATS FACE TOUGH ROAD – News came Tuesday morning as I was writing this blurb that the Kentucky Wildcats would be playing at Tennessee later in the evening
without starting point guard Lamont Butler. Butler has struggled in recent games while battling a nagging shoulder injury, including the disappointing 74-69 loss to Vanderbilt on Saturday afternoon. His stat line reflected that something was amiss. Butler, who has been a solid leader at the point, was just 2-for-7 from the field, uncharacteristically turned the ball over six times, and was not the defensive presence UK fans have gotten accustomed to seeing. He fouled out after playing 27 minutes as well.
Butler was certainly not the only Wildcat to struggle in the Music City. Koby Brea's shooting slump continued – he was only 1-for-4 from 3-point land – and 7-footer Amari Williams, who is perhaps the most confounding player on the team, appeared disinterested at times.
The Cats were playing without starting forward Andrew Carr as well. He remained questionable going into the UT game, and he may be out a significant amount of time. Backup point guard Kerr Kriisa remains out, and his return this season remains a huge question mark.
In addition to the injuries, several of Kentucky's issues in their other losses resurfaced in Memorial Gymnasium, i.e. shoddy defense, handling physicality, getting outhustled for loose balls, and offensive droughts. UK simply did not appear to be ready to play and it may be the first time all year their effort has come into question. That won't get it in Knoxville; a physical dogfight and an elite Volunteer defense were already expected to be factors, and if the Cats don't respond early and often, this one could get ugly for the visitors.
It will be an uphill struggle for the Cats to finish in the top half dozen or so teams in the deep and talented Southeastern Conference, and the team depth will be put to the test during the foreseeable future. This was not an especially deep team to begin with, and getting and staying healthy appears to be a challenge as well.
*****
EAGLES FLYING HIGH IN OVC – The Morehead State Eagles were also in action on Tuesday evening (after this was submitted) hosting Southern Indiana, and hoping to continue its stranglehold on the top spot in the Ohio Valley Conference. The Eagles entered the game undefeated this season at Ellis T. Johnson Arena and 8-2 in OVC play, a game in front of Little Rock and Southern Illinois-Edwardsville.
First-year coach Jonathan Mattox, who took over the program when Preston Spradlin moved to James Madison University after last season, has the Eagles in prime position for a regular-season title, but the big prize comes in the OVC tournament, when the champion receives an automatic bid to the Big Dance.
MSU is 13-8 overall and is led by former Madisonville North Hopkins standout Kenny White Jr, the team's leading scorer and rebounder. The 6-foot-7 senior has posted averages of 13.3 points per game and has grabbed 6.5 rebounds per outing. Former George Rogers Clark star guard Jerone Morton, who led GRC to its first state title since 1951, has been seeing increased minutes and is tossing in 11.7 points per game.
Morehead State's next home game is Thursday night, when Tennessee Tech, coached by former UK Unforgettable John Pelphrey, visits Johnson Arena. The Eagles will be looking to
avenge a 74-55 defeat to the Golden Eagles in Cookeville on Jan. 4.
*****
LET THE HYPE BEGIN – With Super Bowl LIX set for Sunday, Feb. 9 in New Orleans, that gives the national pundits and so-called experts ample time to come up with storylines and speculation about the participants, the two-time defending champion Kansas City Chiefs, and the Philadelphia Eagles.
We will have more to say as the clash, also known as SB 59 draws nearer, but the early betting line has installed KC as a 1.5-point favorite. Apparently, most of the so-called experts are picking the Chiefs to three-peat, but you can bet most of America is rooting for the Eagles to soar and spoil the party for Patrick Mahomes and company.
Lots of fans are getting tired of the Chiefs, which is a natural reaction to a team that wins and wins and wins some more. Many fans buy into the conspiracy theory that the NFL wants the Chiefs to win, which is just ridiculous. Coach Andy Reid and his team simply have a knack of performing their best under pressure, and he and his players deserve a tremendous amount of credit.
I would not be the least bit surprised to see Kansas City make it three in a row, but I expect the Eagles to perform at an extremely high level. If you recall two years ago, Philly seemingly was on its way to knocking off the Chiefs in Super Bowl LVII, but Mahomes rallied his team to a 38-35 victory. Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts arguably outplayed the Kansas City QB in that one, but the Chiefs overcame a 24-14 halftime deficit to pull out the win. Hurts was 27-for-38 for 304 yards
and a touchdown through the air, and rushed for three more scores and 70 yards.
One player who was not a member of that Eagles team should play a prominent role and perhaps lead Philadelphia to a victory. That of course is running back Saquon Barkley, who has had a magnificent season in the City of Brotherly Love.
*****
'I like information. I love when smart people make me think of something in a new way.' – Terry Francona
*****
'The church is always trying to get other people to reform; it might not be a bad idea to reform itself a little, by way of example.' — Mark Twain

title: Lady Bears score 104 over Robertson
description: The Bracken County Lady Bears headed to Mt. Olivet to take on the Robertson County Lady Devils on the basketball court Thursday evening.
content:
The Bracken County Lady Bears headed to Mt. Olivet to take on the Robertson County Lady Devils on the basketball court Thursday evening.
Coming into the contest, Bracken County sat at 10-7 on the season, and 3-2 in the district. In the second game of the season for the Lady Bears, they hosted the Lady Devils, coming out with an 87-15 win, and were hoping for another strong showing against Robertson County at their home gym in Mt. Olivet.
Robertson County were 5-10 on the season prior to tipping off with Bracken County, and hoping to bounce back from their loss earlier in the season to head into the final few weeks of 2024-25 prepped and ready to go as the 38th district tournament draws near.
In the first quarter, the Lady Devils fought to keep the game close, holding strong with Bracken County throughout much of the early minutes of the contest. Unfortunately for Robertson County, the Lady Bears defense would hold the Lady Devils to 11 by the end of the first, while the offense put up 31.
'Right now we're just moving forward trying to get ready for the district.' said Lady Bears head coach, Troy Archibald, 'It's late in the season, so we gotta keep playing. It is what it is, we just gotta keep playing, we gotta keep scoring. I don't really know what to say, Our girls just played well, we passed the ball well, we shot well. That's what we've been working on, sharing the ball. I've got three seniors and I'm letting my seniors play.'
Throughout the remainder of the first half, the Lady Bears continued to pull ahead, outscoring the Lady Devils 26-5 to lead 57-16 heading into halftime.
'The team's what it is. We're not as good as we have been in the past couple years. The girls played hard, but we don't have the talent that some of these schools do.' said Lady Devils head coach, John Pilosky, 'All I ask the girls to do is play your hardest. If we get beat 40 or 50, it is what it is, but at least play your hardest. I don't think we're getting that effort out of the girls this time.'
As both teams returned to the court, Bracken County was looking to continue furthering their lead over the Lady Devils, while Robertson County hoped to get back into the contest late in the game.
In the third quarter, Robertson County scored four, with a pair of field goals from Carrie Morgan and Peyton Jolly totalling the Lady Devils' performance on the offensive end. Bracken County put up 21 this quarter to lead 78-20 heading into the final eight minutes of play. As the contest came to a close, the Lady Devils would put up four more in the fourth quarter, as the Lady Bears continued to pull ahead. Bracken County outscored the Lady Devils 26-4 in the fourth, for an 80 point, 104-24 lead at the end of the contest.
'We wanted to play man, like I said we're preparing for the district. We wanted to throw in a press there, to work on that. That's a press we haven't worked on all year. We wanted to start working on a press and we did that. We created turnovers and people got upset, all I can say is it's late in the season and we're preparing for the district. These girls have worked their tails off, I've got girls that's been with me for four years, five years, so, we're just gonna keep playing. It is what it is.' said coach Archibald.
The Lady Devils offense slowed down dramatically in the second half, as the physicality of the contest slowly took its' toll on Robertson County's lineup.
'We're not conditioned very well, and I'll take responsibility for that. We play good at times, but then it seems like we get down 15, 20 points we kinda give up on ourselves.' said coach Pilosky.
Robertson County will return to the court on Tuesday, as they head to Lexington to take on the Sayre Lady Spartans, with tipoff scheduled for 7:30 p.m. The Lady Bears will be back in action this afternoon, as they take on the Covington Holy Cross Lady Indians at Augusta.

title: Lady Royals go undefeated in district play
description: The Mason County Lady Royals hosted the Augusta Lady Panthers in their sixth and final 39th district match-up of the regular season.
content:
The Mason County Lady Royals hosted the Augusta Lady Panthers in their sixth and final 39th district match-up of the regular season.
Mason County was 5-0 in the district prior to their contest with the Lady Panthers, beating Augusta once prior 62-15, the St. Pat Lady Saints twice and reigning 39th district champs, the Bracken County Lady Bears twice. Having already clinched the number one seed for the district tournament, the Lady Royals were eager to pick up another win on the season, and head into the final few weeks of the season 6-0 in the 39th, and 15-6 on the season.
Augusta entered the contest 2-3 in the district, and were hoping for an even 3-3 when they left the floor of the Fieldhouse, but faced a tough opponent in the surging Lady Royals.
In the first quarter, Mason County picked up a strong early lead, outscoring the Lady Panthers 22-14. Laci Tackett led the Augusta offense this quarter, with eight points scored across two threes and a field goal. Rounding out the remainder of the Lady Panthers' scoring this quarter were then Ashlyn Sergent with two, Reagan Tackett with three and Kenzington Hinson with one.
The Lady Royals were led this quarter by Kyleigh Kirk, who put up 11 across three threes, and a field goal. Carlee Buttery then put up six, Ceara Fox two, Adrienne Downs-Perry two and Amirah Reed one to close out Mason County's scoring.
'Tonight because we were so much smaller, we just kinda focused on being five out and when driving lanes would be there we were looking for that. We were trying to get some paint touches and get some inside out looks. We got them there off some little screens, I don't know how many assists we got tonight but it was nice, the ball was shared well tonight.' said Lady Royals head coach, Jay Fite.
Despite getting down early, and heading into the second quarter trailing by eight, the Lady Panthers stayed confident they could keep the game close throughout the remainder of the contest.
'It was nip and tuck, and we played our style. We wanna play some pressure defense in the full court, and we wanna play man to man. We were kinda shorthanded on the bench tonight, so we had to play a little bit of zone there, because we were winded. We didn't have a lot of girls to go in there.' said Lady Panthers head coach, Todd Kelsch.
Throughout the remainder of the first half, Mason County continued to try and further their lead over the Lady Panthers, while Augusta fought to stay close to the Lady Royals, hoping to get out ahead late in the contest.
The Mason County offense in the second quarter was dominated by Reed, who put up all of the Lady Royals' 18 points this quarter. Reed scored four threes, two field goals and two free throws, once again proving her strength on the offensive end for Mason County.
'She made some nice cuts.' said coach Fite, 'We've always got confidence in Amirah to do that, and even when she does miss a couple we want her to just remember to stay confident and the next one's gonna fall.'
Augusta put up ten more in the second quarter to head into halftime down 40-24, hoping to stage a second half comeback and keep the game close throughout the remaining 16 minutes of play.
As the two teams returned to the court after halftime, both continued to play tough on both ends of the court. The Augusta defense was working hard to slow down the Lady Royals' scoring, while Mason County hoped to continue furthering their lead.
Unfortunately for the Lady Panthers, Mason County once again outscored them this quarter 16-12, getting up 56-36 for a 20 point lead heading into the final quarter of the contest. Augusta's short bench slowed down the offense dramatically in the fourth quarter. With fatigue setting in, the Lady Panthers put up four in the fourth quarter, with a field goal from Hinson and a pair of free throws from Reagan Tackett totalling Augusta's scoring.
Mason County put up 19 in the final eight minutes of play, with Reed once again leading the charge with seven.
By the end of the game, the Lady Royals had built up a 35 point lead, taking the victory 75-40.
'For the first two and a half quarters, I felt like we played really well. Mason County shot the ball really well. I thought we did a pretty good job on Kirk and Reed there to start the third quarter then, Hughes goes in from the three point line. They played like the warriors tonight, I thought we played pretty well. I see some improvement on our team, I'm liking what I'm seeing.' said coach Kelsch.
Now 6-0 in the district and 15-6 on the season, the Lady Royals are eager for their seven remaining regular season games.
'We kinda told our kids at the end of the first quarter, any dead ball situation we want to try to make sure we're able to extend things and not have it slide back. We've had some moments where we've had some comfortable leads and some people have gotten back into some basketball games so we wanted to make sure tonight that we closed that and made sure that people didn't get back in the game.' said coach Fite, 'Just pleased with our kids effort, especially short with not having Lexi, just proud of our kids effort, establishing some things on the defensive end first and then with the ability to knock down some shots.'

title: Archers compete at Bracken County
description: All five local archery teams took to Brooksville this past weekend to compete in the Bracken County Polar Bear Shoot, Bracken County's first home archery tournament.
content:
All five local archery teams took to Brooksville this past weekend to compete in the Bracken County Polar Bear Shoot, Bracken County's first home archery tournament.
Coming in just behind Pendleton County and Simon Kenton, the Fleming County Panthers placed third as a team scoring a combined 3,252, and with 142 tens scored throughout the course of the day.
In the high school boys' division, junior Carson Thomas led the Panthers, putting up a personal best 292, to place second individually out of 70 archers in contention.
Following him was Logan Bretz, with a 275, tying with Robertson County's Wyatt Curtis and Calvin Whalen. Both Bretz and Curtis had 12 tens, the pair tying for eighth. Kevin Alfrey, Eli Cline and John Graham closed out Fleming County's top five in the division, with Alfrey putting up a 268 taking 19th, and both Cline and Graham tying with a score of 266, taking 23rd and 24th respectively.
Mackenzie Conley led the team in the high school girls' division, shooting a personal best 289 to take first place out 86 archers in the field.
Not far behind her, was Terri Applegate, shooting a 285 to take third, and Kaylee Crawford with a 277 to place eighth. Maria Humphries then shot a 260 to take 37th, and Bella Hamilton a 258, tying with Alexis Pendleton, taking 41st, rounding out the Lady Panthers top five archers.
The Mason County Royals then came in right behind Fleming County, placing fourth as a team with a combine 3,247 and 137 tens scored.
Mason County senior Bryce Pollitt led in the division, shooting a 294 to take first place individually.
Dillon Mitchell wasn't far behind, taking seventh place with a score of 277. Jace Dodson then shot a 274 to take 11th, with Dalton Hargett and Jacob Applegate closing out the Royals' top five this event. Hargett shot a 271 with nine tens to tie with St. Henry's Nolan Townsend, taking 16th place. Applegate tied with fellow Royal, Chancellor Trimble with a 269, but shot three more tens, taking 17th.
Laurelle Setters led Mason County in the high school girls' division, taking 17th with a score of 271. Mary Katherine Shepherd then shot a 270, placing four spots behind Setters at 21st. Closing out the Lady Royals' top five were then Kimber Ferguson at 27th with a 266, and Sydney Hamilton and Eden Abshire, both shooting 261s with eight tens, tying with Pendleton County's Elizabeth Ammerman. Hamilton took 33rd, and Abshire 34th.
The Robertson County Black Devils were the next highest scoring local team, placing sixth, just behind St. Henry. The Black Devils scored a combined 3,083, picking up 83 tens throughout the course of the day.
Wyatt Curtis and Kalvin Whalen led the team in the high school boys' division. Both archers shot 275, Curtis' personal best. Curtis shot one more ten than Whalen, tying with Fleming County's Logan Bretz, placing eighth, with Whalen taking 10th.
Chris Jett, Andrew Gray and Henry Chain then wrapped up Robertson County's top five archers in the division. Jett shot a personal best 267 with 13 tens to place 21st, Gray a 262 to place 32nd and chain a 260 to place 39th.
In the high school girls' division, Zoey Earlywine led Robertson County, shooting a 269 placing 22nd. Liz Murell then shot a 259 to take 39th, with Marley Emmons, Zoey McKay and Nicole Godsey closing out the top five for the Lady Devils. Emmons placed 54th, shooting a 252, McKay 58th, with a score of 251 and Godsey 68th, shooting a 245.
The last local team competing for team placement, was then the Augusta Panthers, taking seventh with a team score of 2,925 and 65 tens.
Jasper Miller led the Panthers in the high school boys' division, shooting a personal best 268 with nine tens to tie with Fleming's Kevin Alfrey, placing 20th. Cayden Bach then also shot a personal best 263 to take 30th, with Tristen Price, Camden Gill and Ayden Courts closing out the Panthers' performance this meet. Price shot a 242 to take 55th, Gill a 214 to take 66th and Courts a 209 to place 68th.
In the high school girls' division, Augusta was led by Adalen Gilliam, with a personal best 260 placing her 36th. Nora Gill then shot a 252, taking 55th, with Abbey Bradford not far behind with a 251, placing 57th. Claire Elliott then close out Augusta's performance in the division, with a personal best 235 placing her 72nd.
While they were not competing for team placement, tournament hosts the Bracken County Polar Bears were competing as individuals.
In the high school boys' division, Bracken County was led by Levi Botkin, with a 272 placing him 14th. Cayden Williams then shot a 231 to take 60th, with Landen Bishop just behind him a 61st, shooting a 227. Bracken County's last archer competing in the high school boys' division was then Colby Moore, shooting a 180 to place 70th.
Anna Bond led the Lady Bears with a 265, placing 28th. Bracken County's top five in the high school girls' division was then rounded out by Ellie Gallagher, Grace Scott, Sanae Takata and Sheyla Torres-Marquez. Gallagher shot a 241 placing 69th, with Scott shooting a personal best 235 to take 71st, Takata a 230 to take 73rd and Torres-Marquez a 229 to place 74th.
Each archer competing this past weekend worked hard to help their team place high in the standings, and to place as high as possible individually. Their hard work and dedication to the sport continues to help them improve as the season progresses, with several local teams heading to Mt. Oliver to compete in the RCS NASP IBO/3D Challenge next weekend.

title: Hello, March! What took you so long?
author: Chuck Hamilton
description: Ah, the third month of the year is here at last.
content:
Ah, the third month of the year is here at last.
Our long, at times brutal winter is behind us, and it is finally time to get outdoors a bit more and enjoy everything that goes with the busy month of March. It's true that the weather is not always ideal during the month; temperatures will rise and fall, chilly winds will be gusting, and winter is not quite finished in our little corner of the universe.
Spring is drawing nearer however, and there is much to celebrate during March. For sports fans, there is the obvious. We have what will assuredly be a wild and unpredictable March Madness, with this year's 68-team field being announced on Sunday, March 16.
Opening Day in Major League Baseball will follow just a couple of days after Selection Sunday with the Tokyo Series pitting the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers against the Chicago Cubs for a pair of games at the Tokyo Dome on Tuesday, March 18, and Wednesday, March 19. Cincinnati will celebrate what should still be the first game of the season on Thursday, March 27, when they open the Terry Francona era at 4:10 p.m. against the San Francisco Giants.
Other happenings during March include Mardi Gras, with Fat Tuesday festively celebrated on March 4, the final day of feasting before the Lenten season. That is followed by Ash Wednesday on March 5, the beginning of Lent, a 40-day period of fasting and prayer leading up to Easter.
We spring our clocks forward on Sunday, March 9 to leap into Daylight Savings Time, something that should go away permanently, in this guy's humble opinion. There has been talk in some states about eliminating the silliness and going to either standard or daylight time on a permanent basis, but so far on the federal level, we wait as Congress drags its heels.
St. Patrick's Day is the next big event, and the 'Wearing of the Green' falls on a Monday this year. Everybody is Irish on March 17, the anniversary of the death of Ireland's patron saint in 461. Despite being
born in Roman Britain, Patrick was kidnapped and enslaved in Ireland at the age of 16. He escaped six years later and returned to Britain, where he had a vision that led him to study for the priesthood, and he returned to Ireland to spread Catholicism. He was later venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church, the Lutheran Church, the Church of Ireland, and the Eastern Orthodox Church.
Coming up in the early morning on Thursday, March 20 is something many of us have been eagerly anticipating. That's right, spring will be arriving, and not a moment too soon. That doesn't mean every day will be sunny and warm, but it does signify that at the very least, winter is officially over.
A quick personal note to wrap up our segment about March, before finally delving into a few sports items. With today being the first day of the third month, happy birthday wishes go out to an old friend, Chris Coney. Have a good one, and many more!
*****
CATS FACING OLD NEMESIS – Bruce Pearl brings his No. 1-ranked Auburn Tigers to Lexington this afternoon in search of an elusive victory against the Kentucky Wildcats. In his career at Tennessee and Auburn, Pearl is 10-18 against the Cats, and 0-6 versus UK in Rupp Arena as the Tigers head coach. Overall, Auburn is a paltry 2-51 in Lexington, with the most recent win a 53-52 upset of then-No. 1 Kentucky on Jan. 9, 1988.
All of that is ancient history now.
Pearl has had the Tigers playing excellent basketball consistently throughout the season. They are coming into this showdown with a 26-2 record, and an impressive 14-1 mark in the brutal Southeastern Conference. Auburn will be seeking its sixth consecutive win and at least a share of the SEC regular season crown.
Kentucky (19-9, 8-7 SEC) is coming off a wild 83-82 win at Oklahoma on Wednesday that saw Otega Oweh will the Cats to the victory in the late stages of the back-and-forth affair. Oweh, playing at his former school and getting booed the entire game, banked in the eventual winning
shot in the lane with 6.4 seconds left, and blocked a shot seconds later to hold off the Sooners' upset bid. He scored the Wildcats' final 18 points and finished with a career-high 28, bouncing back from his season-low output of two points in the 96-83 loss at Alabama.
The game in Norman also marked the return of the Cats' starting guard tandem of Lamont Butler and Jaxson Robinson, with mixed results. Butler, who remains integral to any success enjoyed by UK down the stretch and in the postseason, scored seven points and dished out six assists before fouling out. Robinson also tossed in seven points, but left the game in the first half after re-aggravating the injury to his right wrist. Butler is expected to start at the point against Auburn, but Robinson is questionable.
The Cats will need everyone in the lineup to play at the top of their respective game, and a hot-shooting performance from beyond the 3-point line would go a long way in achieving an upset. A win over the top-ranked team in the nation would go a long way to ensuring a high seed in the postseason for Kentucky, and as usual, it could come down to how well the home team defends and rebounds against the tough-minded Tigers, who are led by Morehead State transfer Johni Broome.
The 6-foot-10 senior is being touted as a prime candidate to be named the National Player of the Year, and he leads Auburn in points, rebounds and assists. He's averaging 18.8 points, 11 boards and 3.4 assists per game.
The Tigers are far from a one-man show however, with six players scoring in double-digits on the season.
Chad Baker-Mazara, a 6-7 senior and at times a controversial figure on the court, is tossing in 12.7 ppg and leads the ball-hawking Tigers defense in steals. Senior point guard Denver Jones (11.0), senior guard Miles Kelly (10.9), freshman guard Tahaad Pettiford (10.7), and 6-7 senior forward Chaney Johnson (10.4) add point production to a squad averaging 85.1 points per game while shooting 48.4% from the field.
It's obvious that Pearl has a deep and loaded team this season, and one that will be difficult to handle for the Cats, even though the fans will be
in a rowdy and supportive frame of mind. Auburn is unbeaten on the road in the SEC, with their lone conference loss coming at home to Florida, 90-81. Their other defeat was at Duke, an 84-78 loss to the Blue Devils on Dec. 4.
The game represents a monumental opportunity for Kentucky to chalk up another win over a Top 15 team, and it would be the first win for he Cats over a No.1-ranked opponent since a 69-62 victory over Michigan State on Nov. 5, 2019 in the Champions Classic at Madison Square Garden. Today's game vs. Auburn also marks a chance for Mark Pope to make history. If UK wins, he would be the first Kentucky head coach in his first season to defeat an AP top-ranked team in the regular season in school history.
*****
BAT CATS OFF TO SIZZLING START – Another sure sign of spring is the beginning of the college baseball season, which actually began in mid-February.
Kentucky, with a revamped roster following a 46-16 season and its first appearance in the College World Series last summer, is 6-1 in the early going. The Bat Cats swept a three-game series at Belmont last weekend before returning to Kentucky Proud Park for its home opener vs. Evansville on Tuesday. The team certainly lived up to its nickname, getting their bats warmed up to score seven runs in the first inning on their way to a historic offensive explosion.
When the dust settled, the Bat Cats had rolled to a 24-3 win, the most runs ever scored by a Nick Mingione-coached team. It was the most runs UK had scored in a game since 2014, and the sixth-most in school history.
As you would expect, numerous UK players contributed to the onslaught, with 13 players scoring runs, and 13 driving in at least one run. Kentucky hosted Morehead State on Wednesday, and won its fifth consecutive game, 8-2.
Cole Hage, a transfer from Columbia University, has been on an early tear for the Bat Cats. The senior utility player leads the team with 12
hits, 11 runs scored, and a .545 batting average. Freshman shortstop Tyler Bell leads UK with nine RBI, and the Illinois native is hitting .370 with four doubles and a 437-foot home run to his credit. A couple of seniors, infielder Patrick Herrera and catcher Devin Burkes, are hitting .400 and .316, respectively. Carson Hansen, a junior outfielder who transferred from Wisconsin-Milwaukee, has clubbed a pair of dingers in limited action. He is 4-for-8 at the plate and scored five runs.
The pitching staff has been terrific as well. Nic McCay, a senior righthander from South Dakota State, is 2-0 in 11 innings on the hill, and has allowed only one unearned run while striking out 11. Southpaw Ben Cleaver is 1-0 in his two starts with a 1.86 ERA, and the lanky sophomore has fanned 16 batters in 9 2/3 innings.
*****
REDS ADDING ANOTHER STARTER? – As you may have ascertained in previous columns, I always enjoy seeing MLB trade rumors, especially when they mention the Cincinnati Reds.
Here's one I just came across this morning, and it involves the Reds possibly adding another starting pitcher to the mix, since Andrew Abbott and Rhett Lowder are currently sidelined, and veteran lefty Wade Miley won't be ready until May at the earliest.
This rumor states that three pitchers – Jose Quintana, Kyle Gibson, and Spencer Turnbull – are likely to secure big league deals, even though it's getting rather late in the offseason. Whether or not any of the trio could give the Reds rotation a significant boost is debatable, but adding another veteran starter could potentially help a young staff.
*****
'It was one of those March days when the sun shines hot and the wind blows cold; when it is summer in the light, and winter in the shade.' – Charles Dickens
*****
'The proverb says that Providence protects children and idiots. This is really true. I know because I have tested it.' — Mark Twain
